title: Running Open Knowledge
description: How Open Knowledge works, its two deployment modes — a stateless library served from a public git repository, or a full instance with pseudonymous accounts and certificates — and exactly how to deploy each, step by step.

questions.text: What fundamentally distinguishes static content mode from database mode?

choices.text: Static mode renders a public git repository with no server state; database mode keeps state (accounts, progress, certificates) in SQLite
Static mode is read-only for visitors; database mode lets visitors edit courses
They are different applications with different interfaces

questions.explanation: One codebase, one env var: with OK_CONTENT_REPO set the instance becomes a stateless renderer of a public repository; without it, it runs the full stateful experience with identities and an admin panel.

questions.text: How do you publish new content in static mode?

choices.text: Edit the files, commit, and git push — the site updates within about a minute
Redeploy the application container
Upload the files through the admin panel

questions.explanation: Git is the admin panel in static mode. The instance caches content for about sixty seconds, so a push goes live without touching the deployment.

questions.text: Why can static mode run on serverless platforms while database mode cannot?

choices.text: Static mode keeps no server state, so wiped filesystems don't matter; database mode needs a persistent disk for SQLite and media
Serverless platforms block SQL for security reasons
Database mode uses too much CPU for serverless

questions.explanation: Serverless filesystems are ephemeral. A stateless renderer doesn't care; a database does. Database mode wants one machine, one disk, one instance.

questions.text: In database mode, who administers the instance?

choices.text: The first account registered on the fresh instance becomes the administrator
An account created via a config file with a plaintext password
Anyone who knows the server's IP address

questions.explanation: First registration bootstraps the admin — so register immediately after deploying, and guard the recovery code: with no email on file, it is your way back in.

questions.text: What does registering in database mode require?

choices.text: Nothing personal: you get a pseudonymous identity like Erudito#4821 secured with a TOTP authenticator
A verified email address
A full name and phone number

questions.explanation: Accounts exist only to keep learning state. They hold a pseudonym, credentials, progress and results — the learner is never a product, in either mode.

questions.text: What is the one non-negotiable rule of a database-mode deployment?

choices.text: Mount a persistent volume at /data and run exactly one instance
Use at least three replicas behind a load balancer
Run a managed PostgreSQL cluster

questions.explanation: Everything that matters — database, media, encryption key — lives in /data, and SQLite wants a single writer. Lose the volume, lose the library (which is why the one-click backup zip exists).

questions.text: Why must ids never change once content is published?

choices.text: Visitor progress is keyed to course and material ids — changing them resets everyone's progress
Git refuses to commit files whose ids changed
Ids are cryptographically signed

questions.explanation: In static mode progress lives in the visitor's browser keyed by those ids; in database mode, in the server. Either way, renaming ids orphans real people's progress.

questions.text: The MIT license allows selling Open Knowledge-based products. What does the project ask of you?

choices.text: To understand that the license is a floor, not a compass: the intent is libraries given as gifts, not paywalled knowledge products
To pay royalties on commercial deployments
Nothing — the project endorses any use equally

questions.explanation: Permissiveness is how tools spread, and your library depends on nobody's permission. But Open Knowledge was built for the tradition of the public library and free software: give it away.

questions.text: Why do Open Knowledge exams show an explanation after every answer?

choices.text: Retrieval practice with corrective feedback strengthens memory far more than re-reading — exams here are a learning tool, not a filter
To make exams longer and harder to pass
Because scores cannot be computed client-side

questions.explanation: Learning science calls it the testing effect: being made to recall, then immediately corrected, consolidates knowledge better than passive review. The explanation is the most valuable part of the question.
